speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Second Minister for Finance Ms Indranee Rajah and I will be making Ministerial Statements to address the issues raised.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Without intending to, it may have led the public to believe that the Government is changing its policy to allow full NRIC numbers to be exposed on a wide scale.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: NRIC numbers can only be collected when there is a need to do so.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Organisations that collect NRIC numbers also have a duty of care.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Subject to applicable law, they must notify and seek consent on use, and ensure protection of the data.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These are existing guidelines that will not change.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, there are also some incorrect uses of the NRIC number today.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Our plan was to stop these incorrect uses while the problem is relatively contained.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Doing so will better protect everyone and allow us to use NRIC numbers with confidence.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In this regard, my Statement today will address two issues: the current incorrect uses of NRIC numbers and why we need to change; and what our next steps will be.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For organisations that deal with many people, say, a hospital with several patients named John Tan, they need a better way to uniquely identify them.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Their NRIC number is a useful unique identifier in such situations.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: When the hospital needs to perform an operation or dispense medication, the doctor or nurse must make absolutely sure that it is the right John Tan they are dealing with and they should ask you, "What is your NRIC number?" Since the NRIC number's purpose is to be a unique identifier, it cannot be a secret, just as our names are not secret.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I should emphasise, however, that while your NRIC number is not a secret, it is not meant to be widely disclosed.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is the concern echoed in Mr Lim Biow Chuan's question.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We would only disclose our NRIC number under certain circumstances, for example, when required by law.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Some examples include disclosing our NRIC number to our employers, at the clinic or when we subscribe to a mobile telephone line.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Because we do have to disclose our NRIC number to others for such purposes, we must assume that at least some people know our NRIC number.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Over time, however, NRIC numbers have become increasingly used as more than an identifier.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Previously, organisations would require seeing my physical NRIC card to confirm that I am who I claimed to be.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, some organisations assume that if someone can cite my NRIC number, that person must be me!

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: On the assumption that this person is indeed me, some organisations may go further to give the person access to privileged information or services.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: When used this way, my NRIC number is no longer just an ID, or identifier, but a key to unlock more information or services.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In such situations, the NRIC number is being accepted as an authenticator, or proof of who a person claims to be.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Instead of the full NRIC number, some organisations collect and use a partial NRIC number, usually the last four characters of the NRIC number.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They think that this is safe and that revealing only the last four characters still keeps the full NRIC number secret.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Among public agencies, even when the agencies had the full NRIC numbers, the use of masked NRIC numbers became more common.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Besides organisations, some individuals also started to use their NRIC numbers as their passwords.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The easy availability of such algorithms means that the continued use of partial or masked NRIC numbers gives both organisations and individuals a false sense of security.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This does not really keep the full NRIC number secret.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This also makes the practice of using NRIC numbers as passwords even more inappropriate.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To the questions by Dr Tan, Mr Liang Eng Hwa and Ms Sylvia Lim, these developments led the Government to take steps to stop the incorrect uses of the NRIC number.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This meant two things: one, not using the NRIC number as an authenticator; and two, moving away from the use of masked NRIC numbers, because it creates a false sense of security.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But it was better to start while the problem is relatively contained and for the Government to take the lead.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To the question by Ms Joan Pereira, we proceeded to ask agencies to stop using the NRIC number as an authenticator or as a password.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We also asked agencies not to plan new uses, with a view to discontinuing existing uses of masked NRIC numbers eventually.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In hindsight, what we should have made clear was that moving away from the use of masked NRIC numbers did not mean automatically using the full NRIC number instead, in every case.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In place of masked NRIC numbers, in some instances, there would be no need for the NRIC number at all.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In other instances, names alone or some other identifier would be sufficient.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But there could also be instances where full NRIC numbers should be used, instead of masked NRIC numbers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Each case would have to be assessed and decided individually.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Members including Mr Leong Mun Wai, Mr Liang Eng Hwa, Mr Xie Yao Quan, Ms Jessica Tan, Mr Dennis Tan and Mr Pritam Singh have asked about the internal processes leading to ACRA's actions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Minister Indranee will say more about it in her Statement later and address Members' questions related to ACRA.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Miss Cheryl Chan asked why the efforts to change did not include the private sector.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Government knew that it would take time for public agencies to make the change.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We expected that it would take even longer for the private sector because of long-standing practices and habits.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The plan was therefore to change the internal practices of Government before moving to change practices in the private sector and non-profit organisations, which Ms Usha Chandradas asked about.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We believed that doing so would allow us to better understand the implementation challenges and, as a result, facilitate a smoother transition in the private sector.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We had also planned to mount a major effort to help Singaporeans be aware of the risks and to support efforts to stop incorrect practices.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Bizfile incident was an unfortunate misstep which now means these plans need to be brought forward.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: While we had taken steps to stop the incorrect uses of NRIC numbers in the public sector, we had not started implementation for the private sector.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Edward Chia, Mr Liang Eng Hwa, Ms Hazel Poa and Mr Xie Yao Quan have asked specifically what should be done in the private sector.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Our initial soundings with the private sector suggest there can be different approaches.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Some organisations currently using partial NRIC numbers can stop the practice and replace them with alternative means of identification such as mobile numbers or email addresses or drop them entirely.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But there are also organisations that need to accurately identify persons and can justify the collection of full NRIC numbers even if they are not required by law.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For example, preschool centres will prefer to collect the full NRIC numbers of visitors rather than just the mobile numbers; the parents will certainly feel more secure.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In applications for and disbursements of substantial financial aid, persons would also need to be accurately identified.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We will take these considerations on board when updating the guidelines.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In any case, I would like to assure Members like Ms Jean See and Mr Ong Hua Han that the Personal Data Protection Commission will support businesses in changing their authentication methods.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This will include raising their awareness on why the use of NRIC numbers as a factor of authentication is unsafe and working through the Infocomm Media Development Authority and the Cyber Security Agency's programmes to help businesses review and adjust their practices.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To questions by Ms Tin Pei Ling, Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim and Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, I should emphasise that NRIC numbers are personal data.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This means that organisations collecting and using NRIC numbers must continue to exercise a duty of care.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Subject to applicable law, they must notify and seek consent on use, and also ensure the data is sufficiently protected.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Certainly, they should not disclose the NRIC numbers unless there is good reason to do so.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Members may also ask, if the NRIC number is not suitable as an authenticator, what about the physical NRIC card, our pink identity card?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If we look at our physical NRIC card, we will see that it contains other identifying information, such as our photo and fingerprint.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It allows others to check that the information on the card matches me, the person holding the card.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In addition, the physical NRIC card is not easily faked.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The physical NRIC card is, therefore, suitable as an authenticator, or proof of who I claim to be.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But someone providing my NRIC number and claiming to be me, does not have these additional factors of proof.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Organisations must know that the physical NRIC card and NRIC number are different.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Organisations should, therefore, not accept my NRIC number alone as proof that the person citing it is indeed me.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Besides organisations, individuals, too, have questions about what they should do.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The first is to clarify their understanding of the NRIC number.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Members like Ms Sylvia Lim asked about this.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We have said that our NRIC number is like our name.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Even if it is not widely disclosed, it is not secret.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In our daily lives, if someone we do not recognise calls out our name and starts to behave as though they know us well, we would be slightly suspicious.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We might be polite but not too friendly.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Certainly, we should not fully trust this person, just because they know our name.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This should also be how we treat anyone who tells us our NRIC number.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We should not automatically assume that they know us well or are figures of authority or can be trusted.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We should be cautious about revealing more about ourselves, or saying yes to their requests or following their instructions without checking further.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The second thing we can do as individuals is to review our passwords.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If we have used our NRIC number as a password to access any information or service, we have mistakenly used it as an authenticator and should change the password immediately.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Doing so will give us better protection against people who use our NRIC number to get access to information or services.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It will also complement efforts by organisations to stop using the NRIC number as a factor of authentication.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To Ms Hany Soh's question, NRIC-related scams are not new.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Most NRIC-related scams involve victims who think they are speaking to figures of authority and end up taking actions that harmed themselves, such as transferring money without further checks.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Very few cases have involved scammers directly using NRIC numbers to unlock access to valuables.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Several Members have also asked how to mitigate the risks when NRIC numbers are disclosed.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They include Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim, Mr Edward Chia, Mr Christopher de Souza, Mr Ong Hua Han, Mr Liang Eng Hwa, Ms Jessica Tan, Mr Louis Chua, Miss Cheryl Chan, Mr Sharael Taha and Mr Yip Hon Weng.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As I have explained, the risks arise from the incorrect use of the NRIC numbers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If individuals stop using NRIC numbers as passwords and organisations stop using NRIC numbers as authenticators, this will go a long way to preventing harms from scams and identity theft.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They will give us all better peace of mind to use the NRIC number whenever it is necessary, such as to get medical treatment or apply for jobs.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Our public education efforts will raise awareness among organisations and individuals, and to guide them on what they should do.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In doing so, we will focus on the points I highlighted above.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Gerald Giam asked about alternatives to the current NRIC number system.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In fact, the risks do not arise directly from the structure of the NRIC number.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Rather, the risks arise when the NRIC number, which is meant to be a unique identifier, is incorrectly used as an authenticator or a password.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Even if we were to create an alternative identifier, we would still have a problem if organisations used it as an authenticator and individuals used it as a password.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These were raised by Ms Tin Pei Ling, Ms Sylvia Lim, Mr Saktiandi Supaat and Mr Patrick Tay.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Government has always taken seriously its responsibility to protect the data entrusted to the public sector.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Government's personal data protection standards are set collectively by the Public Sector (Governance) Act, or PSGA, and our own internal rules.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The PSGA is aligned with the PDPA and adapted to the Public Service context.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Our internal rules are comprehensive and take reference from international and industry standards.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We also continually strengthen our data governance practices.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: ACRA is expected to comply with these rules and the PSGA, which are no less stringent than PDPA requirements.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Regular, mandatory audits are conducted to ensure that public agencies, including ACRA, comply with the standards for data protection and the security of information and communications technology systems.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The number of data incidents and their severity is published annually.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In the most recent whole-of-Government audit exercise on information technology-related data security controls, there were very few significant findings and all of them had been remediated by the agencies concerned.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: There has also been a reduction in data incidents of medium severity and above.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Where necessary, we have also taken public servants to task, for example, in serious cases involving unauthorised disclosure or improper use of information.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Members can be reassured that we take these rules and controls very seriously.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We will continue to regularly review the safeguards to ensure that they remain relevant.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Subject to law, they must notify and seek consent on use, and ensure protections.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These are existing guidelines that will not change.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These include using NRIC numbers for authentication or as passwords.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is better to make these changes while the problem is relatively contained.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Organisations and individuals can both help by taking steps to stop using NRIC numbers as authenticators or passwords.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: By taking action as soon as possible, we can increase protection for all of us.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This will allow us to more confidently use the full NRIC number as a unique identifier whenever we need to do so.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, the Government understands the public's concerns about the correct use of NRIC numbers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: NRIC numbers are personal data, and they can only be used and disclosed when there is a need to do so.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Unless indicated by law, organisations that wish to collect and hold your NRIC number must first notify and seek consent on its use, and ensure that it receives adequate protection.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, what needs to change are some incorrect uses of the NRIC number.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The Second Minister for Finance will indeed also be making a related Ministerial Statement.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I will allow Members to raise points of clarifications on both Statements after Minister Indranee's Statement.
